planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring or fall in acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; site a male pollinator near female plants for berry set.

directions: Set container-grown plants in spring or fall into acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, placing a male pollinator near female plants for fruit set. Perny's holly is native to mountain forests of central and western China and carries unusually small, nearly square leaves with only a few widely spaced marginal spines, giving the plant a fine, almost boxwood-like texture quite different from coarser American and English hollies. Growth is notably slow, so allow several seasons for plants to fill in, and expect light crops of small red berries on mature female specimens in winter. Because of its refined foliage this species has long served as a breeding parent for hybrid hollies such as Ilex x aquipernyi, and it makes a good specimen or slow-growing hedge where a dense, small-scaled evergreen is wanted.

planting.note: Plant in spring into well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial sun; protect from hard freezes, as this species is tender compared to most landscape hollies.

directions: Plant in spring into well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial sun to light shade, and protect young plants from hard freezes since this is one of the more cold-tender hollies in general cultivation. Native to the Ryukyu Islands of Okinawa, this dwarf species gets its name from its two distinct leaf forms: juvenile growth bears small, spiny-toothed leaves, while mature wood produces tiny, smooth-edged, glossy leaves on compact, densely branched stems. The fine scale of its foliage and naturally twiggy habit have made it a favorite subject for bonsai growers, who prize its slow growth and tight internodes. In the ground it stays a compact mounding shrub for many years, useful in containers or sheltered borders in warm climates where its lack of hardiness is not a concern.

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; this Chinese species is still mostly found through specialty and collector nurseries.

directions: Plant container-grown specimens in spring or fall into moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, where this woodland species is most at home. Native to the mountain forests of central China, Farges' holly carries narrow, lance-shaped leaves that are largely smooth along the margins rather than toothed or spined, a trait shared by only a handful of hollies and one that sets it apart visually from spiny-leaved relatives like Ilex cornuta. Female plants produce small red fruit in fall following insignificant white spring flowers. It remains uncommon outside botanic garden collections and specialty holly or conifer nurseries, so give it time to establish and avoid heavy pruning while the plant is young and slow to recover.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; needle juniper tolerates poor, rocky ground once established.

directions: Plant container-grown trees in spring into well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun, where the loose, open branching shows to best effect. Native to Japan, Korea, and northeastern China, needle juniper keeps sharp, true needle-like foliage its whole life rather than switching over to flattened scale leaves as most junipers do with age, giving it a softer, more textured look from a distance despite the foliage being quite prickly up close. Branches arch outward and the branchlets droop gracefully at the tips, producing a weeping, almost willowy silhouette that has made the species a long-favored subject for bonsai as well as specimen planting. Once established it tolerates drought, wind, and poor rocky soil, and needs little care beyond occasional shaping.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; this slow-growing conifer needs years to develop its narrow pyramidal form.

directions: Plant container-grown trees in spring into well-drained, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun, giving the tree room to develop its dense, narrow, pyramidal crown over many years. Native to mountain slopes of Greece, Turkey, Lebanon, and Syria, this juniper is unusual in bearing its sharp needle-like leaves in whorls of three rather than the paired or scale-like arrangement typical of most junipers, which packs the branches with an unusually dense, bristly texture. Female trees produce large, fleshy, blue-purple seed cones that resemble small plums, far bigger and more conspicuous than the berries of other junipers, which is the source of the species name drupacea. It is slow to grow and best sited on a well-drained slope or rocky bank where water does not stand, and it is prized among conifer collectors for its distinctive texture and conspicuous fruit.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; this slow conifer is grown mainly through specialty conifer nurseries and collector seed exchanges.

directions: Plant container-grown trees in spring into well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, in a site sheltered from the harshest winter wind. Native to high-elevation forests of the Himalaya and adjacent western China, this juniper is named for its strongly drooping, recurved branchlets, which hang from the branches to give the whole tree a soft, weeping outline unlike the stiffer habit of most junipers. Scale-like blue-green foliage covers the pendulous shoots, and old specimens develop a gnarled, picturesque trunk. In its native range, timber from the variety known as coxii was historically prized for coffin-making in Bhutan and Tibet. Growth is slow, and plants are still found mainly through specialty conifer nurseries and collector seed exchanges rather than general garden centers.

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in lean, well-drained, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; a tough Mediterranean conifer for hot, dry sites.

directions: Plant container-grown plants in spring into lean, well-drained, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun, on a hot, open site that mimics its native Mediterranean scrubland. Native across Spain, Portugal, southern France, Greece, and North Africa, prickly juniper carries stiff, sharply pointed true needles rather than scale leaves, arranged in pairs along reddish-brown stems whose bark splits and peels in thin shreds with age. The wood of this species was historically distilled to produce cade oil, long used in traditional skin treatments, leather tanning, and as a smoky flavoring agent. It is exceptionally drought tolerant once established and shrugs off poor, rocky, alkaline soils that defeat most other woody ornamentals, making it a durable choice for xeric Mediterranean-style plantings.
